tests_declared: Dynamic flexion-extension MRI of cervical spine

resident.chief_complaint: Progressive unsteadiness and bilateral lower limb weakness over six months, now unable to walk without a walking aid.
resident.history: Fifty-one-year-old delivery man with no significant past medical history presented with progressive unsteadiness and bilateral lower limb weakness over six months, worsening to inability to walk without a walking aid. He also had chronic neck stiffness for over two years and had not sought intervention. He denied any difficulty with hand dexterity, such as using chopsticks, buttoning a shirt, or picking up a coin.
resident.physical_exam: Neurological examination revealed signs of myelopathy in the lower limbs. MRC muscle power grading in both lower limbs (L2-S1) was 4/5. Deep tendon reflexes, including knee jerk and ankle jerk, were exaggerated bilaterally. Babinski's sign was positive bilaterally. The patient had difficulty getting up from an armless chair and was unable to perform tandem gait. No upper limb signs were demonstrated: sensory-motor function and reflexes were normal in both upper limbs, and Hoffman's sign was negative.
key_positive_signs: Exaggerated knee and ankle deep tendon reflexes bilaterally
Difficulty rising from an armless chair
resident.past_history: No significant past medical history. Chronic neck stiffness for over two years, for which he did not seek intervention.
resident.public_message: A 51-year-old man presented with six months of progressive unsteadiness and bilateral lower limb weakness, now requiring a walking aid, and chronic neck stiffness for over two years. Examination showed bilateral lower limb weakness (MRC 4/5), exaggerated knee and ankle reflexes, bilateral Babinski signs, difficulty rising from a chair, and inability to tandem gait; upper limbs were neurologically normal. JOA score was 14/17 (grade 1 disability). Cervical spine X-rays showed degeneration with loss of lordosis and anterior osteophytes C3-C6; CT and MRI showed extensive OPLL from C3 to T3 causing significant canal compromise with no cord signal changes. Diagnosis: extensive cervicothoracic OPLL causing myelopathy.

imaging.public_message: Reporting the case record’s description only; the films were not available for review. CT and MRI were described as showing extensive ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL) from C3-T3 with significant canal compromise. No cord signal change was reported. The direction of compression and a graded severity of stenosis were not stated. The described imaging has high correlation with the reported myelopathic symptoms.

neurology.localization: The examination localizes to an upper motor neuron lesion above the lumbosacral enlargement, consistent with myelopathy. Bilateral lower limb weakness with exaggerated knee and ankle reflexes, and positive Babinski signs indicate corticospinal tract dysfunction. The absence of upper limb motor, sensory, or reflex abnormalities and a negative Hoffman sign, together with no documented sensory level or sphincter disturbance, means the clinical level cannot be pinpointed to the cervical cord alone; it is compatible with lower cervical or upper thoracic cord involvement. The OPLL from C3 to T3 provides a structural correlate. Lower-limb-predominant myelopathy is well recognized in OPLL because the laterally placed lower-limb fibers in the corticospinal tract and the longest axons are most vulnerable to anterior compression. The examination is incomplete as lower limb sensory function, sensory level, and sphincter function are not documented.

red_flags.finding: Normal upper limb motor/sensory/reflexes and negative Hoffman despite OPLL from C3.
red_flags.rationale: Lower-limb-predominant myelopathy is common in OPLL because the lower-limb corticospinal fibers are more laterally placed and more vulnerable to anterior compression, and early disease often spares the upper limbs. This does not offer an alternative cause and does not change the levels already identified by imaging.

red_flags.finding: No cord T2 signal change on MRI.
red_flags.rationale: Absence of T2 hyperintensity does not exclude clinically significant myelopathy, especially in early or dynamic compression. It is not an alternative explanation and does not alter the indication; it may suggest less severe cord damage but does not change the plan.

red_flags.finding: Incomplete documentation of lower limb sensory exam, sensory level, and sphincter function.
red_flags.rationale: The missing data limit precise clinical localization and cannot confirm a sensory level matching the imaged OPLL. However, the upper motor neuron signs already establish a myelopathy above the lumbosacral enlargement, so this gap does not change the diagnosis or the surgical plan.

neurology.symptom_imaging_mismatch: There is no fundamental mismatch: the imaging shows extensive C3-T3 OPLL with canal compromise that can explain the bilateral lower limb upper motor neuron syndrome. Notable but non-contradictory observations are the absence of upper limb signs despite C3 involvement and absent cord signal change; both are consistent with early, leg-predominant cervical/thoracic myelopathy. The exact symptomatic level cannot be determined from the examination because lower limb sensory level and sphincter function were not documented.
neurology.public_message: The examination localizes to an upper motor neuron lesion above the lumbosacral enlargement, consistent with myelopathy; the absence of upper limb signs means the clinical level is likely lower cervical or upper thoracic, not definitively C3. The imaging shows extensive C3-T3 OPLL with canal compromise, which explains the dominant lower-limb syndrome; the symptom-imaging match is high. Notable findings are all coexisting and do not change the indication or plan: (1) normal upper limbs despite C3 involvement—common in early leg-predominant OPLL; (2) no cord T2 signal—does not exclude myelopathy; (3) incomplete sensory/sphincter documentation—limits precise level but not diagnosis. There is no evidence of coexisting peripheral neuropathy or central sensitization.

anesthesia.public_message: ASA grade III. Intraoperative MAP target 75 mmHg. Expected blood loss risk moderate. Prone position tolerance moderate. Extubation difficulty unassessable: no airway assessment on record.

preconditions_for_failure: Worsening of lower limb weakness or gait instability, such as new falls or inability to walk even with an aid
Development of new upper limb symptoms, sphincter dysfunction, or a drop in JOA score by 2 or more points
No stabilization or improvement of neurological status after 3 months of structured conservative treatment
Evidence of new or progressive cord signal change on follow-up MRI
physiatrist_opening.public_message: I acknowledge that progressive myelopathy carries a risk with delay. However, the absence of cord signal change on MRI and the relatively preserved JOA score (14/17) leave a narrow window for a time-limited, closely monitored conservative trial. A structured program of physical therapy, gait training, activity modification, and serial neurological assessments could be offered for 3-6 months, provided the patient is fully informed and there is immediate access to surgical evaluation if any failure criterion is met. This approach is not without risk, but surgery for extensive OPLL also carries significant morbidity, and early intervention may still be possible if deterioration occurs.

physiatrist_final.public_message: The Director has not ruled and is ordering further studies, not pointing to a specific finding I have underweighted. The Deputy Director's statement that delay risks irreversible deficit repeats the progressive myelopathy I already weighed; no new finding from the record has been identified that changes that balance. I hold my position that a time-limited, closely monitored conservative trial remains a rational option.

vice_opinions.assessment: This 51-year-old man has progressive cervical/upper thoracic myelopathy (JOA 14, worsening gait) caused by extensive OPLL from C3 to T3 with significant canal compromise. The six-month progression with new walking aid dependence is a clear surgical indication. Absence of T2 cord signal change does not reduce the risk of irreversible deterioration, and a conservative trial would expose the patient to that risk without likely benefit. Surgical decompression should be planned now. Given the multilevel extent and pathology, a posterior approach is the most defensible strategy.
proposed_options: Posterior decompression (laminectomy) and instrumented fusion from C2 or C3 to T3, covering the full extent of significant OPLL canal compromise.
Posterior cervical laminoplasty C3-C7 plus thoracic laminectomy T1-T3 without fusion, reserving fusion for later if kyphosis develops.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Posterior decompression and instrumented fusion from C2/C3 to T3
disagreement_points: I disagree with the physiatrist's proposal for a 3-6 month conservative trial. Progressive myelopathy from OPLL is a surgical disease; delay risks irreversible cord damage, and JOA 14 does not provide a safe observation window.

The radiology description lacks critical parameters (canal occupancy, cord compression ratio, OPLL morphology, sagittal alignment). I would not finalize surgical planning without direct review of the imaging by the operating surgeon.
deferred_questions_to_director: Please review the CT and MRI yourself to confirm the most cephalad and caudal extent of significant cord compression, the direction of compression, and whether there is associated cervical kyphosis.
Do you prefer the fusion to end at C7 (with thoracic decompression only) or continue to T2/T3 given the documented OPLL extent? Your judgment on instrumentation length is requested.
vice_opinions.public_message: From a spine surgery perspective, this is progressive myelopathy from extensive OPLL requiring surgical decompression. I favor a posterior decompression and instrumented fusion across the involved segments. I do not support a conservative trial. Final planning should await your review of the imaging and decision on surgical extent.

vice_opinions.assessment: This is a 51-year-old man with progressive cervical/upper thoracic myelopathy due to extensive OPLL C3-T3 causing significant canal compromise. The clinical picture—progressive lower-limb weakness, hyperreflexia, Babinski signs, gait deterioration—is classic for upper motor neuron dysfunction and correlates with the imaging. Although there is no T2 cord signal change and JOA is only modestly reduced (14/17), the progression over six months is concerning and supports surgical decompression rather than observation. I agree with the Director that final operative planning requires personal review of imaging with quantitative stenosis, a dynamic flexion-extension MRI to assess kyphosis/instability, and formal airway assessment. My current surgical preference remains posterior decompression and instrumented fusion across the involved segments, assuming acceptable sagittal alignment and no severe kyphosis; if dynamic imaging reveals significant kyphosis or instability, a combined anterior-posterior approach may be needed, though the morbidity of anterior OPLL resection must be weighed.
proposed_options: Posterior decompression (laminectomy/laminoplasty) with instrumented fusion from C3 to T3 (possibly extending to C2 and/or upper thoracic) for non-kyphotic or mildly kyphotic alignment, with intraoperative neuromonitoring.

Combined anterior-posterior decompression and fusion if dynamic MRI demonstrates severe kyphosis (>13 degrees), segmental instability, or OPLL with >50-60% canal occupancy where posterior-only decompression would be insufficient; anterior approach could be corpectomy with OPLL resection or anterior floating method.

Posterior decompression without fusion (laminoplasty) only if lordosis is preserved, no instability, and OPLL is not occupying >50% canal; however, given extensive disease and progressive myelopathy, fusion is generally preferred.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Posterior decompression and instrumented fusion (C3-T3, with possible C2 extension) provided dynamic MRI shows no severe kyphosis and posterior decompression is deemed adequate.
disagreement_points: I disagree with Rehabilitation Medicine's proposal for a time-limited conservative trial. Progressive myelopathy even without T2 cord signal change indicates surgical decompression; delay risks irreversible neurological deterioration, and the relatively preserved JOA score should not be used to justify observation.

The threshold for proceeding with anterior surgery in extensive OPLL needs scrutiny. A combined anterior-posterior approach carries higher morbidity (dysphagia, CSF leak, graft complications), and posterior-only decompression with fusion and possible lordosis restoration may be adequate even with moderate kyphosis; I would challenge an automatic switch to combined surgery based solely on dynamic MRI findings.

The extent of fusion—whether to instrument to C2, whether to cross the cervicothoracic junction, and how far into the thoracic spine to extend—remains unsettled and should be determined by the quantitative stenosis and dynamic imaging.
deferred_questions_to_director: After reviewing imaging, what are the quantitative stenosis parameters (canal occupancy, OPLL type, K-line, degree of kyphosis) at the most compressed levels?
What does the dynamic flexion-extension MRI show regarding instability or reducible kyphosis?
What is the anesthesia airway assessment, and if difficult, is a fiberoptic plan in place?
What is your final decision on surgical approach and fusion extent once all data are available?
vice_opinions.public_message: Director, I concur that surgical decompression is indicated in principle for this progressive myelopathy. My recommendation remains posterior decompression and instrumented fusion across the involved segments, contingent on the imaging review and airway assessment. I do not support a conservative trial; the clinical progression is clear, and delay risks irreversible deficit. I will await your review and the additional studies before we finalize the plan.

delegated_tasks: Radiologist: perform quantitative re-analysis of existing CT and MRI (canal occupancy, cord compression ratio, OPLL morphology, sagittal alignment) and report on the new dynamic flexion-extension MRI
Anesthesiologist: perform formal airway assessment and report on safety of prone positioning with optimized hemodynamic plan

director_rulings.reason_for_delay: Awaiting direct imaging review and formal airway assessment before deciding between surgical decompression and a time-limited conservative trial; patient safety requires complete objective data.
director_rulings.public_message: The department has not reached consensus. As director, I consider surgery indicated in principle for progressive myelopathy caused by extensive OPLL, but I am not prepared to rule on the operation today. Before any final recommendation, I need to personally review the imaging with quantitative stenosis parameters and have a formal airway assessment from anesthesia. I also want the rehabilitation medicine's proposed conservative trial evaluated against objective data. I am therefore ordering a dynamic flexion-extension MRI and an anesthesia airway evaluation. If the airway assessment reveals a difficult airway, we will not proceed without a documented fiberoptic plan; if the imaging demonstrates severe kyphosis, a combined anterior-posterior procedure may need to be reconsidered. We will reconvene after these results are available.

director_rulings.final_decision: The meeting is closed for additional workup. Surgery is indicated for progressive myelopathy caused by extensive OPLL, but the final operative decision is deferred until dynamic flexion-extension MRI and a formal anesthesia airway assessment are completed and reviewed. Posterior decompression and instrumented fusion remains the preferred low-risk plan if the workup confirms no prohibitive kyphosis or instability. If severe kyphosis is found or a difficult airway is identified, we will not proceed without a revised, lower-risk plan or reconsideration of conservative management. The department will reconvene after the results are available.
delegated_tasks: Radiologist: perform dynamic flexion-extension MRI and provide quantitative canal occupancy, OPLL type, K-line, and degree of kyphosis.
